opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question we debate a lot internally, and I don't think there's a single right answer. It depends on what you're modeling and what you want the model to do downstream.

Language is naturally discrete. Words and tokens are symbols, so autoregressive models over discrete tokens fit it very well. The physical world is different. Images, video, motion, and physics are fundamentally continuous signals. When we build models that try to understand and simulate the world, we have to decide whether to force that continuous signal into a discrete vocabulary or to model it directly in continuous space.

Discrete representations have real advantages. You can reuse the whole large-language-model machinery: next-token prediction, cross-entropy loss, and well-understood scaling behavior. It also becomes much easier to mix modalities, because once video is a sequence of tokens, it can sit in the same sequence as text and actions. The cost is quantization. Every time you discretize, you lose some information, and for visual data that loss shows up as artifacts, blurriness, or temporal flicker. You also need a very good tokenizer. In practice the tokenizer often becomes the ceiling on quality.

Continuous representations, like the latent spaces used in diffusion models, usually preserve much more detail. That's why diffusion has been so strong at visual quality. The trade-off is that integrating them with language-style reasoning is less straightforward, and sampling can be more expensive, although distillation and better solvers have narrowed that gap a lot.

So my practical view is this. If the priority is fidelity, meaning photorealistic, physically plausible video for simulation or for generating training data for robots and autonomous vehicles, continuous latents with diffusion tend to win today. If the priority is reasoning, planning, or tight integration with a language model, discrete tokens are very attractive. That's why we've explored both families rather than betting on one. Increasingly I think the answer will be hybrid: a model that reasons in a more discrete, symbolic space and renders or predicts in a continuous one.

A good tokenizer, discrete or continuous, matters underneath all of this. People pay a lot of attention to the big backbone, but how you compress the world into a representation in the first place quietly determines much of what the model can learn. Getting that compression right is one of the most underrated problems in the field.

r001.rationale: The response compares representation choices by task priorities and suggests a hybrid approach, but it does not argue that the model best suited for deployment is the one most likely to succeed.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because it's really not a question you can answer in the abstract. It depends on what the data looks like, and it depends on what you want to do with it.

Let me start with the obvious case. Language is inherently discrete. Words are tokens, there's a finite vocabulary, and there's no meaningful notion of "halfway between two words." So for language, a discrete representation with an autoregressive model is a very natural fit. You predict the next token, you sample from a categorical distribution, and the whole machinery works beautifully. The success of large language models is partly a success of matching the architecture to the nature of the data.

Now, video and images are different. Pixels are continuous. The physical world is continuous. When a car moves across the frame, it doesn't jump between discrete states, it moves smoothly. So my instinct for visual data is that continuous representations are more faithful. Diffusion models operate in that continuous space, and they can capture fine-grained details and subtle variations that are hard to represent once you've quantized everything into a codebook.

But here's the tension. Discrete tokens have practical advantages that are hard to ignore. First, they let you reuse all the infrastructure that was built for language models. The transformers, the training recipes, the scaling laws, the serving systems. If you tokenize video, you can treat it as just another sequence and plug it into the same pipeline. Second, discrete tokens make it much easier to build multimodal systems. If text is tokens and video is tokens, then mixing them in one model is straightforward. That's very attractive if your goal is a model that can reason across modalities, not just generate pretty pictures.

The cost of going discrete is information loss. Tokenization is a compression step, and compression throws things away. If your tokenizer is weak, the model downstream can never recover what was lost, no matter how big it is. So a lot of the quality of a discrete video model lives in the tokenizer, and people sometimes underestimate how hard it is to build a good one.

Continuous models, on the other hand, keep more of the signal, and I think for the highest fidelity generation they still have the edge today. The cost is that they're often slower to sample, and integrating them with language and reasoning is less natural.

So how do I actually choose? I ask what the downstream use case is. If I want the best possible visual quality, say for simulation or for generating training data for a robot, I lean continuous. If I want a model that can take instructions, reason about a scene, and tie that reasoning back to language, discrete tokens make that integration much easier.

And honestly, in practice I don't think it's either-or. At NVIDIA we've built both, and I see them as complementary. You can have a discrete model that is good at understanding and planning, and a continuous model that is good at rendering the details, and have them work together. I suspect over time the boundary will blur even more, with hybrid approaches, or tokenizers that are rich enough that the distinction stops mattering as much. But right now, the honest answer is that discrete buys you convenience and composability, continuous buys you fidelity, and you pay for whichever one you give up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing based on the downstream use case and weighs fidelity against convenience and composability. It does not argue that the best model for deployment is ultimately the one most likely to succeed.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what structure does the representation need to preserve? Discrete representations are useful when you want a compact vocabulary and a sequence that a model can predict token by token. But quantization introduces a tradeoff—you can lose fine details, and the choice of codebook matters.

Continuous representations make it easier to preserve subtle variations, which is valuable for images and video. They also fit naturally with diffusion models, although you still have to decide how much to compress the signal and where to spend computation.

So I wouldn’t choose one in isolation. I’d look at reconstruction quality, generation quality, inference cost, and how the representation connects to the rest of the system. A hybrid can also make sense: discrete representations for higher-level structure, with continuous representations for the details.

r001.rationale: The response recommends comparing reconstruction and generation quality, inference cost, and system fit, but it does not say that the best deployment model is ultimately the one most likely to succeed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the choice should follow the structure of the problem. Discrete representations are useful when you want a compact vocabulary of reusable units. For generation, they also let you formulate the task as predicting a sequence of tokens. But quantization introduces a bottleneck: you have to decide which distinctions to preserve and which to discard.

Continuous representations give you more flexibility to preserve fine detail and model smooth variation. The challenge then is learning a distribution over that space and choosing an effective generation process.

So I would look at reconstruction quality, generation quality, computational cost, and how the representation connects to the rest of the system. I also wouldn’t treat this as a strict either-or decision. You can use discrete representations for some aspects of a problem and continuous representations for others, if that gives you a better tradeoff.

r001.rationale: The response compares representation tradeoffs and says the choice should follow the problem’s structure, but it does not argue that the best deployment model is the one most likely to succeed.
